test_cases.name: As a Metro by T-Mobile authorized dealer, I want to activate a store-stock phone while the customer keeps their existing number from another carrier, so that the port is accepted, the old carrier is shown and no extra charge appears up to the payment screen
test_cases.custom_requirements:
## What this test is about
When a customer comes into a Metro by T-Mobile store to start service, they can take a brand-new Metro phone number or keep the number they already have with another carrier. Keeping the number is called porting it in. On the Phone number selection screen the rep picks Port phone number and types the customer's current number, the account number and the PIN the customer has with the old carrier, each twice to catch typing mistakes. RT Go then asks the carrier whether that number can be moved. If it can, the order carries on exactly like a new-number order: protection, plan, promotions, add-ons, create subscriber, order summary, accessories and payment. The port itself costs nothing. Getting this wrong loses the customer their number or activates them on a number the carrier refuses, so the port details must be checked, shown back to the rep and carried through to the payment screen unchanged. This test walks the whole thing with a phone from store stock and a number the carrier reports as Verizon: the port is accepted, the carrier details are shown in the cart drawer, the port-specific rebate is offered, and the order reaches the payment screen with the same amount as a new-number order. It stops before any money is taken.

Words used in this test: a line activation is the sale that puts a phone on the Metro network for a customer. The rep is the store employee at the counter. Porting (or a port-in) means moving a phone number the customer already has with another carrier over to Metro, so the customer keeps the number. The old carrier is the company the customer is leaving; to allow the move, that carrier needs the customer's account number and the account PIN with them. An IMEI is the 15-digit serial number of a phone. A SIM number (also called ICCID) is the long number printed on the SIM card. A plan code such as MAU55 is the carrier's short name for a monthly plan. A rebate is money taken off the phone's price when a promotion applies. Store stock means a phone the store sells from its own inventory, as opposed to a phone the customer already owns.

## What this test is about
When a customer comes into a Metro by T-Mobile store to start service, they can take a brand-new Metro phone number or keep the number they already have with another carrier. Keeping the number is called porting it in. On the Phone number selection screen the rep picks Port phone number and types the customer's current number, the account number and the PIN the customer has with the old carrier, each twice to catch typing mistakes. RT Go then asks the carrier whether that number can be moved. If it can, the order carries on exactly like a new-number order: protection, plan, promotions, add-ons, create subscriber, order summary, accessories and payment. The port itself costs nothing. Getting this wrong loses the customer their number or activates them on a number the carrier refuses, so the port details must be checked, shown back to the rep and carried through to the payment screen unchanged. Not every number can be moved: the carrier refuses some of them. This test types a number the carrier refuses, checks the refusal message and that nothing typed is lost, then corrects the number to one the carrier accepts and checks the order moves on. An IMEI is the 15-digit serial number of a phone. A SIM number (also called ICCID) is the long number printed on the SIM card. ## What this test is about
When a customer comes into a Metro by T-Mobile store to start service, they can take a brand-new Metro phone number or keep the number they already have with another carrier. Keeping the number is called porting it in. On the Phone number selection screen the rep picks Port phone number and types the customer's current number, the account number and the PIN the customer has with the old carrier, each twice to catch typing mistakes. RT Go then asks the carrier whether that number can be moved. If it can, the order carries on exactly like a new-number order: protection, plan, promotions, add-ons, create subscriber, order summary, accessories and payment. The port itself costs nothing. Getting this wrong loses the customer their number or activates them on a number the carrier refuses, so the port details must be checked, shown back to the rep and carried through to the payment screen unchanged. Sometimes the customer decides at the counter to take a new number after all. This test chooses Port phone number, types the port details, then chooses New phone number again and checks the port boxes are gone and the new-number boxes are back, then chooses Port phone number once more and checks the port boxes come back empty. Nothing is submitted to the carrier.

Words used in this test: a line activation is the sale that puts a phone on the Metro network for a customer. The rep is the store employee at the counter. Porting (or a port-in) means moving a phone number the customer already has with another carrier over to Metro, so the customer keeps the number. The old carrier is the company the customer is leaving; to allow the move, that carrier needs the customer's account number and the account PIN with them. An IMEI is the 15-digit serial number of a phone. A SIM number (also called ICCID) is the long number printed on the SIM card. A plan code such as MAU55 is the carrier's short name for a monthly plan. A rebate is money taken off the phone's price when a promotion applies. Store stock means a phone the store sells from its own inventory, as opposed to a phone the customer already owns.
